 # Pathland Project - AI Agent Guide
 
 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.
 
 **Last Updated**: August 14, 2026
 
 ---
 
 ## New Direction: Rust WASM Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine compiled to WASM** ("WASM guest engine")
 > that emits the application's **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack,
 > Text, spacing, padding, alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer**
 > into shared linear memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and
 > modifiers are written in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API; other languages consume
 > the components as **WASM/WIT** components.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors).
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`STYLE` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### Rust Workspace (`lib/rust/`)
 
 ```
 crates/pathland-opcode/   # 16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, memory layout (no_std)
+crates/pathland-view/     # SwiftUI-style view DSL: VStack/HStack/Text + decoupled
+                          #   modifiers (spacing/padding/fontSize/color/background) (no_std)
 crates/pathland-engine/   # retained view tree -> declarative TREE/STYLE opcodes,
                           #   diff-based reactive emission (zero-alloc steady state)
 crates/pathland-host/     # host reader: ring -> native-element description (std layer)
 wit/pathland.wit          # WIT component-world definitions (Goal 3+)
 ```
 
 - Test: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all crates).
 - WASM build: `RUSTC=~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustc cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`
   (the Homebrew `cargo` on PATH uses a rustc without the wasm std; use the rustup toolchain's rustc).
 
 ### POC Goals (issues #12–#16)
 
 | # | Goal | Status |
 |---|------|--------|
-| 12 | 16-byte opcode engine | **In progress** (`feature/opcode-engine` branch) |
-| 13 | Core components & modifiers in Rust | Planned |
+| 12 | 16-byte opcode engine | **Complete** |
+| 13 | Core components & modifiers in Rust | **In progress** (`pathland-view` DSL; defer signals) |
 | 14 | TypeScript browser demo via WASM/WIT | Planned |
 | 15 | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo | Planned |
 | 16 | Rust desktop app with GTK4 renderer | Planned |
 
 ---
 
 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust WASM opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the New Direction section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic
 
 ---
 
 ## Protocol Quick Reference
 
 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | STYLE | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment |
 
 ### Component Types (u16)
 
 | Component | ID |
 |-----------|----|
 | HSTACK | 0x0001 |
 | VSTACK | 0x0002 |
 | TEXT | 0x0003 |
 | BUTTON | 0x0004 |
 | IMAGE | 0x0005 |
 | SWITCH | 0x0006 |
 | TEXT_FIELD | 0x0007 |
 | SPACER | 0x0008 |
 | SCROLLVIEW | 0x0009 |
 | LIST | 0x000A |
 | GRID | 0x000B |
 | COMMENT | 0x000C |
 
 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, JUSTIFICATION=0x0003, PADDING=0x0004, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
 **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D  
 **Style**: COLOR=0x100A, FONT_SIZE=0x1007, FONT_WEIGHT=0x1008, FONT_FAMILY=0x1009, BACKGROUND_COLOR=0x1001, BORDER_WIDTH=0x1003, BORDER_COLOR=0x1004, BORDER_RADIUS=0x1005, OPACITY=0x100D, VISIBLE=0x100E, Z_INDEX=0x100F, CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=0x1010, PADDING_TOP/RIGHT/BOTTOM/LEFT=0x1012-0x1015  
 **Special**: WIDTH=0x100B (use -1=FILL, -2=HUG_CONTENT), HEIGHT=0x100C  
 **Semantic**: ROLE=0x2001, STATE=0x2002, ENABLED=0x2003, SELECTED=0x2004
 
 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent and overrides. Renderer defines visual appearance and behavior.
 
 - Renderer owns design tokens, default values, semantic-token resolution, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme logic
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 
 Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system).
 
 ---
 
 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-opcode/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-engine` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-engine`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-opcode` encoding/emitters
 3. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-engine`/`pathland-host` + tests
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-opcode`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ---
 
 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |
 
 ---
 
 ## Project Status
 
-**Complete**: 16-byte opcode engine (`pathland-opcode`), declarative diff-based reactive emission (`pathland-engine`), host reader to a native-element description (`pathland-host`), golden conformance vectors (incl. raw-input EVENT bytes), typed raw-input event encode/decode, `no_std` + wasm32 builds, zero-alloc steady-state emission. **31 tests green across 3 crates.**
+**Complete**: 16-byte opcode engine (`pathland-opcode`), SwiftUI-style view DSL with decoupled chainable modifiers (`pathland-view`), declarative diff-based reactive emission (`pathland-engine`), host reader to a native-element description (`pathland-host`), golden conformance vectors (incl. raw-input EVENT bytes), typed raw-input event encode/decode, `no_std` + wasm32 builds, zero-alloc steady-state emission. **39 unit tests green across 4 crates.**
 
-**Planned / deferred**: full SwiftUI-style view DSL + signals (Goal 2/#13), TS browser demo via WASM/WIT (Goal 3/#14), Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo (Goal 4/#15), GTK4 desktop renderer (Goal 5/#16), raw-input event routing into the guest engine, TEXT_FIELD editing, image rendering.
+**Planned / deferred**: signals (Goal 2/#13), TS browser demo via WASM/WIT (Goal 3/#14), Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo (Goal 4/#15), GTK4 desktop renderer (Goal 5/#16), raw-input event routing into the guest engine, TEXT_FIELD editing, image rendering.
 
 ---
 
 ## Quick Start
 
 1. Read this file and `spec/OPCODE.md`
 2. Run tests: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all crates)
 3. Build for wasm32: `RUSTC=~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustc cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`
 4. Make small changes, verify they work
 
 ---
 
 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the reference implementation (`pathland-opcode`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

parts.text:
Now let me create the pathland-view crate. I'll design it carefully.

Key design:
- `Node` struct and `Component` enum move here from engine.
- `View` trait with `build(&self) -> Node`.
- `ViewModifier` trait with `apply(&self, node: &mut Node)`.
- `Modified<V, M>` wrapper.
- Builder structs: `VStack`, `HStack`, `Text`.
- Core modifier structs: `Spacing`, `Padding`, `FontSize`, `Color`, `Background`.
- Sugar methods on `View`.
- `assign_ids` internal.

Let me think about the Node/Component design. Currently:

```rust
pub struct Node {
    pub id: u32,
    pub component: Component,
    pub children: Vec<Node>,
    pub width: Option<f32>,
    pub height: Option<f32>,
    pub properties: BTreeMap<u16, u32>,
}

pub enum Component {
    VStack { spacing: f32, padding: f32 },
    HStack { spacing: f32, padding: f32 },
    Text { text: String },
    Spacer,
}
```

The engine's `component_type_id` maps Component → u16.

Now, for the DSL, modifiers apply properties via the `properties` map. But spacing/padding for stacks currently live in the `Component` enum fields. If a user does `VStack::new().spacing(8)`, where does spacing go? Options:
- Put spacing/padding into the `properties` map via the modifier. But then the engine's `reconcile_node` reads `spacing`/`padding` from `Component`, not from `properties`. 

Hmm. Let me think about how emission works. In engine `reconcile_node`:
- For new nodes: emits component spacing/padding if present (via `Component::VStack { spacing, padding }` fields), then emits all `node.properties`.
- For changed nodes: diffs `p.spacing != spacing`, `p.padding != padding`, and generic property diffs.

If the DSL puts spacing into `properties`, the engine needs to handle SPACING property generically. It already does emit `node.properties` via `guest.set_property(node.id, *prop, value_type_for(*prop), *value)`. So if spacing is a property, it will be emitted. But the Component also has spacing field — if we keep both, we'd double-emit.

Cleanest approach: keep `Component` without spacing/padding fields? But that changes engine significantly. Alternatively, keep Component as-is and have `build()` put spacing into the Component field for stacks, and padding likewise, when the view is a stack.

But modifiers are decoupled — `.spacing()` can apply to any view, including Text. Per "allow-and-ignore", `.spacing()` on a Text just sets `properties[SPACING]`. On a VStack... it should set spacing. But where?

The issue: Component::VStack has `spacing` as a field. The generic `properties` map also holds SPACING potentially. If both are set we double-emit in the "new node" path (spacing field emits once, then properties loop emits SPACING again).

I think the cleanest architecture, keeping engine changes minimal and honoring the decoupled modifier model:

**Make Component carry NO spacing/padding.** Instead, all constraint properties (SPACING, PADDING, plus modifiers) live in `node.properties`. This is actually more consistent with the declarative protocol: properties are properties. The `Component` enum becomes purely the *component type* (VStack, HStack, Text, Spacer).

But that's a bigger refactor of the engine's `reconcile_node` which currently reads `Component::VStack { spacing, padding }`. Let me look at how much depends on that.

Engine usage of Component fields:
- `component_type_id` — maps to u16 (fine).
- `reconcile_node`: destructures `Component::Text { text }`, `Component::VStack { spacing, padding } | HStack { spacing, padding }` → gets (text_borrowed, spacing, padding). Emits spacing/padding properties for new nodes and diffs them.

If I change Component to:
```rust
pub enum Component {
    VStack,
    HStack,
    Text { text: String },
    Spacer,
}
```

Then engine `reconcile_node` would only handle text from Component, and spacing/padding come purely from `node.properties`. That actually simplifies the engine: the snapshot would track `properties` generically (it already does — `properties: BTreeMap<u16,u32>`), and text separately. The special spacing/padding snapshot fields could be removed and folded into the generic properties diff.

Wait, but there's a subtlety: the engine currently keeps `text` as a separate field because text lives in the arena (String) not a u32 property. Text via `SET_TEXT`. So `text` stays as a Component field or becomes a property? `SET_TEXT` uses arena; properties use u32 payload. Text can't be a u32 property (strings need arena). So keep text in Component.

So new Component:
```rust
pub enum Component {
    VStack,
    HStack,
    Text { text: String },
    Spacer,
}
```

Engine changes:
- `component_type_id` simplifies.
- `reconcile_node`: extract `text_borrowed` from Component::Text only; drop spacing/padding special-casing; rely on generic `properties` diff for SPACING/PADDING and all modifiers.

This actually makes the engine MORE generic and matches the protocol better. The `SnapshotNode` loses `spacing`/`padding` fields and keeps `properties` (generic). Text diffing unchanged.

Let me re-examine engine's reconcile to make this clean. Current snapshot fields: component_type, parent, index, text, spacing, padding, width, height, properties, gen.

New snapshot: component_type, parent, index, text, width, height, properties, gen. And width/height — currently Node has width/height fields. In the DSL, width/height could be modifiers too (WIDTH/HEIGHT properties). But there are no width/height modifiers in scope #13. Keep Node.width/height as-is for now (engine handles them specially via emit_size_props). Actually wait — should width/height also become properties? The plan says foundation modifiers are spacing/padding/fontSize/color/background. Width/height are "Special" properties (WIDTH=0x100B, HEIGHT=0x100C) handled specially. Node keeps width/height fields; engine continues handling them. Fine — leave Node.width/height.

Hmm, but if modifiers write to properties map and Node also has width/height fields, there's a split. For #13 scope, keep it simple: modifiers write to properties map; Node.width/height remain as-is (used by engine). No width/height modifiers in scope.

Now the DSL. Let me design concretely.

```rust
// view.rs
pub trait View {
    fn build(&self) -> Node;
}

pub trait ViewModifier {
    fn apply(&self, node: &mut Node);
}

pub struct Modified<V, M> {
    pub view: V,
    pub modifier: M,
}

impl<V: View, M: ViewModifier> View for Modified<V, M> {
    fn build(&self) -> Node {
        let mut node = self.view.build();
        self.modifier.apply(&mut node);
        node
    }
}
```

Blanket `.modifier()` on View:
```rust
pub trait ViewExt: Sized {
    fn modifier<M: ViewModifier>(self, m: M) -> Modified<Self, M> {
        Modified { view: self, modifier: m }
    }
    // sugar
    fn spacing(self, v: f32) -> Modified<Self, Spacing> { ... }
    ...
}
impl<T: View> ViewExt for T {}
```

Wait, but `Spacing` is a type; `.spacing(8.0)` returns `Modified<Self, Spacing>`. Good.

Node needs to be built with ids assigned. In SwiftUI the tree is built by `build()` returning Node. But ids: currently engine requires stable unique sequential ids. The legacy TS assigned ids at node creation via counter. Let me have `build()` assign ids using a global/thread-local counter? But `build` takes `&self` — it's called possibly multiple times (for diffing the app rebuilds the tree each time?). 

Actually, let me think about how the engine consumes this. The engine's `emit(root: &Node, guest)` does diff-based emission against a snapshot, keyed by node.id. So the app builds a tree (with ids), emits, mutates, rebuilds/re-emits. For ids to be stable across rebuilds, the app must assign them deterministically.

The legacy TS approach: `nodeIdCounter` incremented at construction. But that's not stable across rebuilds unless deterministic ordering.

The current engine has `view::assign_ids(root, &mut next)` — pre-order sequential assignment, starting from a seed. The engine tests do:
```rust
let mut root = view::vstack(4.0, 8.0, vec![...]);
view::assign_ids(&mut root, &mut 1);
```
So ids start at 1 (root), children get 2, 3, ... This is deterministic given a fixed tree shape — stable across rebuilds as long as structure is stable. That's the "stable identity" model.

So for the DSL, I'll have `build()` produce a Node with ids NOT yet assigned, and expose `assign_ids(root, &mut next)` like the engine had. OR assign ids inside build via a caller-provided seed. 

Hmm, but the modifier `apply` needs node.id? No — modifiers only touch properties/component. They don't need ids. Ids assigned after full build via `assign_ids`. That's clean: `build()` → tree with id:0 placeholders → app calls `assign_ids(&mut root, &mut 1)` → emit.

But that's a two-step API. SwiftUI just calls `build()`. Let me make `build()` the pure Node producer and keep `assign_ids` as a separate function (moved from engine). Tests can use both. Actually, to keep it ergonomic, I could have build() assign ids automatically with a counter that the app controls via a context. But simplest and matching existing engine contract: keep assign_ids separate.

Wait — reconsider. The engine `emit` uses `node.id` for snapshot. If `build()` returns id:0 for everything, that's broken. So assign_ids is required before emit. Keep it as a public helper in pathland-view. The engine tests already use this pattern.

Now `Component` and `Node`:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq)]
pub enum Component {
    VStack,
    HStack,
    Text { text: String },
    Spacer,
}
```

Wait, should Component keep spacing/padding? If modifiers write to properties map, then a VStack built as `VStack::new().children(...)` with `.spacing(8)` — the Spacing modifier writes `properties[SPACING] = 8.0`. The engine emits it as a generic property. That works IF I change the engine to not special-case spacing/padding from Component. So yes, Component drops spacing/padding.

But hold on — is there a downside? The engine currently special-cases spacing/padding to emit valueType F32. If they move to generic properties, the engine emits them via the properties loop with `value_type_for(prop)`. `value_type_for` returns F32 for SPACING/PADDING. Good.

Now `Node`:
```rust
pub struct Node {
    pub id: u32,
    pub component: Component,
    pub children: Vec<Node>,
    pub width: Option<f32>,
    pub height: Option<f32>,
    pub properties: BTreeMap<u16, u32>,
}
```

Same as before. Good.

Views:

```rust
pub struct VStack {
    children: Vec<Box<dyn View>>,
}
impl VStack {
    pub fn new() -> Self { Self { children: Vec::new() } }
    pub fn children(mut self, children: Vec<Box<dyn View>>) -> Self { self.children = children; self }
    pub fn push(mut self, child: impl View + 'static) -> Self { ... }
}
impl View for VStack {
    fn build(&self) -> Node {
        Node {
            id: 0,
            component: Component::VStack,
            children: self.children.iter().map(|c| c.build()).collect(),
            width: None, height: None,
            properties: BTreeMap::new(),
        }
    }
}
```

Hmm, `children(mut self, children: Vec<Box<dyn View>>)`. The engine's current `view::vstack` used `Vec<Node>`. For the DSL, we want `Vec<Box<dyn View>>` so that sub-views can be modified and passed as trait objects. E.g.:

```rust
VStack::new().children(vec![
    Box::new(Text::new("a").color(0xFF_FF0000)) as Box<dyn View>,
    Box::new(Text::new("b")),
])
```

Since `Modified<Text, Color>` implements View, and `Text` implements View, both can be boxed as `Box<dyn View>`. Good.

Alternatively accept `Vec<Box<dyn View>>` directly. Let me provide both `children(Vec<Box<dyn View>>)` and maybe a `child()` method. Keep it minimal: `children()`.

Actually for ergonomics, I could accept generic `Into<Box<dyn View>>`... but `Text` and `Modified<...>` don't implement a common `Into` unless I add. Simpler: `children(Vec<Box<dyn View>>)`. Users write `Box::new(...)`. That's the pragmatic Rust approach (like `iced`).

`Text`:
```rust
pub struct Text {
    text: String,
}
impl Text {
    pub fn new(text: &str) -> Self { Self { text: text.into() } }
}
impl View for Text {
    fn build(&self) -> Node {
        Node {
            id: 0,
            component: Component::Text { text: self.text.clone() },
            children: Vec::new(),
            width: None, height: None,
            properties: BTreeMap::new(),
        }
    }
}
```

`Spacer` — the engine has Spacer. Is it in scope? The issue says foundation components VStack/HStack/Text. But Spacer exists in Component. Keep Spacer as a view for completeness since Component::Spacer exists. Low cost.

Modifiers:
```rust
pub struct Spacing(pub f32);
impl ViewModifier for Spacing {
    fn apply(&self, node: &mut Node) {
        node.properties.insert(property_id::SPACING, self.0.to_bits());
    }
}
```
etc. `Color` sets `property_id::COLOR`. `Background` sets `property_id::BACKGROUND_COLOR`. `FontSize` sets FONT_SIZE. `Padding` sets PADDING.

Sugar on ViewExt:
```rust
fn spacing(self, v: f32) -> Modified<Self, Spacing> { self.modifier(Spacing(v)) }
fn padding(self, v: f32) -> Modified<Self, Padding> { self.modifier(Padding(v)) }
fn font_size(self, v: f32) -> Modified<Self, FontSize> { self.modifier(FontSize(v)) }
fn color(self, c: u32) -> Modified<Self, Color> { self.modifier(Color(c)) }
fn background(self, c: u32) -> Modified<Self, Background> { self.modifier(Background(c)) }
```

Now, `component_type_id` — moved from engine to view:
```rust
pub fn component_type_id(component: &Component) -> u16 {

For `property_change_emits_only_delta`: they mutate `a.component = Component::VStack { spacing: 12.0, ... }`. Now component is `Component::VStack` with no fields, and spacing is a property. So the mutation should be on `a.properties.insert(property_id::SPACING, 12.0.to_bits())`.

For `node_added_emits_create_and_insert`: `root.children.push(view::text(3, "cd"))` — now we push a text node and need to reassign ids. The old behavior: after first emit, root(1), text1(2), then push text with explicit id 3. With the new DSL, ids are assigned via `assign_ids` which reassigns all. Let me think about how the test should change.

The cleanest approach: build the tree with the DSL, call assign_ids, emit. To mutate, modify the Node structure directly. For adding a child, build a new tree or push a node then reassign ids.

```rust

5. `node_removed_emits_delete`: build with two texts (ids 1,2,3), emit, pop, emit, expect DELETE node 3.

6. `child_reordered_emits_move`: hstack with two texts, emit, swap children, emit, expect 2 MOVE_CHILD.

7. `steady_state_emits_zero`: build, emit twice, empty.

8. `emit_is_zero_alloc_in_steady_state`: build with two texts, assign ids, emit warmup, then steady state zero alloc.

The issue is that when I do `.spacing(4.0)` on a VStack, it returns `Modified<VStack, Spacing>`, and then `.children(...)` isn't available on `Modified`. So the chain `VStack::new().spacing(4.0).padding(8.0).children(...)` fails because after `.spacing()` we get a `Modified`, which doesn't have `.children`.

I need `.children()` before the modifiers in the chain, OR `.children()` should be available on Modified too. The cleanest approach for the DSL: set children first, then modifiers. So `VStack::new().children(...).spacing(4.0).padding(8.0).build()`.

But wait — the order of `.children()` matters for the "innermost first" semantics. Children are structural, not a modifier; setting children first is fine. Let me update all call sites to put `.children()` first.

Actually, in SwiftUI, VStack { ... } sets content as the first argument, then modifiers chain after. So `VStack::new().children(...).spacing(...)` is the natural order. Let me update the tests to match.

36: ## Engine example
37: 
38: The engine emits declarative structure (no rects). A signal changes a property;
39: the next `emit` writes only the delta opcodes.
40: 
41: ```rust
42: use pathland_engine::{view, Engine};
43: use pathland_opcode::{init_memory, Guest, MemoryLayout};
44: 
45: let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
46: let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
47: init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
48: 
49: let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
50: let mut engine = Engine::new();
51: 
52: let mut root = view::vstack(4.0, 8.0, vec![view::text(1, "Hello")]);
53: view::assign_ids(&mut root, &mut 1);
54: 
55: guest.begin_frame();
56: engine.emit(&root, &mut guest).unwrap(); // full structure
57: guest.end_frame();
58: 
59: root.component = pathland_engine::Component::VStack { spacing: 12.0, padding: 8.0 };
60: 
61: guest.begin_frame();
62: engine.emit(&root, &mut guest).unwrap(); // exactly one SET_PROPERTY
63: guest.end_frame();
64: ```
65: 
66: Emission in the steady state allocates nothing; only changed nodes produce
67: opcodes, so an unchanged tree emits zero opcodes. Native renderers map the
68: structure onto their native elements (GTK4 widgets, DOM elements).

POC Goal 2 (#13) implemented. Summary:

**New crate `pathland-view`** (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-view/`)
- `Node`/`Component` moved here from engine (view → engine → host layering)
- `View` trait (`build()`), `ViewModifier` trait (`apply()`), `Modified<V,M>` wrapper
- Core views: `VStack`, `HStack`, `Text`, `Spacer` (builder structs, `.children(...)`)
- Core modifiers: `Spacing`, `Padding`, `FontSize`, `Color`, `Background` — decoupled, apply to any view

 # Pathland Project - AI Agent Guide
 
 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.
 
 **Last Updated**: August 14, 2026
 
 ---
 
 ## New Direction: Rust WASM Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine compiled to WASM** ("WASM guest engine")
 > that emits the application's **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack,
 > Text, spacing, padding, alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer**
 > into shared linear memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and
 > modifiers are written in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API; other languages consume
 > the components as **WASM/WIT** components.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors).
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`STYLE` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### Rust Workspace (`lib/rust/`)
 
 ```
 crates/pathland-opcode/   # 16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, memory layout (no_std)
 crates/pathland-view/     # SwiftUI-style view DSL: VStack/HStack/Text + decoupled
                           #   modifiers (spacing/padding/fontSize/color/background) (no_std)
 crates/pathland-engine/   # retained view tree -> declarative TREE/STYLE opcodes,
                           #   diff-based reactive emission (zero-alloc steady state)
 crates/pathland-host/     # host reader: ring -> native-element description (std layer)
 wit/pathland.wit          # WIT component-world definitions (Goal 3+)
 ```
 
 - Test: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all crates).
 - WASM build: `RUSTC=~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustc cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`
   (the Homebrew `cargo` on PATH uses a rustc without the wasm std; use the rustup toolchain's rustc).
 
 ### POC Goals (issues #12–#16)
 
 | # | Goal | Status |
 |---|------|--------|
 | 12 | 16-byte opcode engine | **Complete** |
 | 13 | Core components & modifiers in Rust | **In progress** (`pathland-view` DSL; defer signals) |
 | 14 | TypeScript browser demo via WASM/WIT | Planned |
 | 15 | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo | Planned |
 | 16 | Rust desktop app with GTK4 renderer | Planned |
 
 ---
 
 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust WASM opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the New Direction section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic
 
 ---
 
 ## Protocol Quick Reference
 
 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | STYLE | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment |
 
 ### Component Types (u16)
 
 | Component | ID |
 |-----------|----|
 | HSTACK | 0x0001 |
 | VSTACK | 0x0002 |
 | TEXT | 0x0003 |
 | BUTTON | 0x0004 |
 | IMAGE | 0x0005 |
 | SWITCH | 0x0006 |
 | TEXT_FIELD | 0x0007 |
 | SPACER | 0x0008 |
 | SCROLLVIEW | 0x0009 |
 | LIST | 0x000A |
 | GRID | 0x000B |
 | COMMENT | 0x000C |
 
 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, JUSTIFICATION=0x0003, PADDING=0x0004, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
 **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D  
 **Style**: COLOR=0x100A, FONT_SIZE=0x1007, FONT_WEIGHT=0x1008, FONT_FAMILY=0x1009, BACKGROUND_COLOR=0x1001, BORDER_WIDTH=0x1003, BORDER_COLOR=0x1004, BORDER_RADIUS=0x1005, OPACITY=0x100D, VISIBLE=0x100E, Z_INDEX=0x100F, CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=0x1010, PADDING_TOP/RIGHT/BOTTOM/LEFT=0x1012-0x1015  
 **Special**: WIDTH=0x100B (use -1=FILL, -2=HUG_CONTENT), HEIGHT=0x100C  
 **Semantic**: ROLE=0x2001, STATE=0x2002, ENABLED=0x2003, SELECTED=0x2004
 
 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent and overrides. Renderer defines visual appearance and behavior.
 
 - Renderer owns design tokens, default values, semantic-token resolution, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme logic
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 
 Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system).
 
 ---
 
 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-opcode/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-engine` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-engine`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-opcode` encoding/emitters
 3. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-engine`/`pathland-host` + tests
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-opcode`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ---
 
 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |
 
 ---

 ---
 
 ## Quick Start
 
 1. Read this file and `spec/OPCODE.md`
 2. Run tests: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all crates)
 3. Build for wasm32: `RUSTC=~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustc cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`
 4. Make small changes, verify they work
 
 ---
 
 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the reference implementation (`pathland-opcode`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

 # Pathland Rust Workspace
 
 The Rust core of Pathland: a **WASM guest engine** that emits the declarative
 view structure as a fixed 16-byte opcode ring buffer into shared linear memory,
 consumed by host renderers.
 
 ```
 crates/
 ├── pathland-opcode/   # 16-byte opcode, ring buffer, bump arena, linear-memory layout (no_std)
 ├── pathland-view/     # SwiftUI-style view DSL: VStack/HStack/Text + decoupled
 │                      #   chainable modifiers (spacing/padding/fontSize/color/background) (no_std)
 ├── pathland-engine/   # retained view tree -> declarative TREE/STYLE opcodes,
 │                      #   diff-based reactive emission (zero-alloc steady state)
 └── pathland-host/     # host reader: ring -> native-element description (std layer)
 ```
 
 ## Specification
 
 - [`spec/OPCODE.md`](../../spec/OPCODE.md) — the 16-byte opcode protocol
 - [`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`](../../spec/CONFORMANCE.md) — golden byte vectors
 
 ## Run tests
 
 ```bash
 cargo test
 ```
 
 ## Build for wasm32
 
 ```bash
 RUSTC=~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustc \
   cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
 ```
 
 > The Homebrew `cargo` on PATH resolves a rustc without the wasm std. Use the
 > rustup toolchain's rustc via `RUSTC=...` (or `rustup run stable cargo`).
 
 ## Engine example
 
 The engine emits declarative structure (no rects). A signal changes a property;
 the next `emit` writes only the delta opcodes.
 
 ```rust
 use pathland_engine::Engine;
 use pathland_opcode::{init_memory, Guest, MemoryLayout};
-use pathland_view::{assign_ids, Text, VStack, View, ViewExt};
-use std::boxed::Box;
+use pathland_view::{assign_ids, text, vstack, View, ViewExt};
 
 let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
 let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
 init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
 
 let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
 let mut engine = Engine::new();
 
-let mut root = VStack::new()
-    .children(vec![Box::new(Text::new("Hello"))])
+let mut root = vstack![text("Hello")]
     .spacing(4.0)
     .padding(8.0)
     .build();
 assign_ids(&mut root, &mut 1);
 
 guest.begin_frame();
 engine.emit(&root, &mut guest).unwrap(); // full structure
 guest.end_frame();
 
 root.properties.insert(pathland_opcode::property_id::SPACING, 12.0f32.to_bits());
 
 guest.begin_frame();
 engine.emit(&root, &mut guest).unwrap(); // exactly one SET_PROPERTY
 guest.end_frame();
 ```
 
 Emission in the steady state allocates nothing; only changed nodes produce
 opcodes, so an unchanged tree emits zero opcodes. Native renderers map the
 structure onto their native elements (GTK4 widgets, DOM elements).

3: //! The Pathland SwiftUI-style view DSL. Core components (`VStack`, `HStack`,
4: //! `Text`) and chainable modifiers (`spacing`, `padding`, `font_size`, `color`,
5: //! `background`) build a retained **view tree** (`Node`) that

7: //!
8: //! ## Decoupled modifiers
9: //!
10: //! Modifiers are **decoupled from views** (SwiftUI-style): any modifier applies
11: //! to any view via the blanket `View::modifier`, and application code composes
12: //! **custom modifiers** from the core ones by implementing `ViewModifier`:
13: //!
14: //! ```

16: //!

Yes. The DSL (`pathland-view`) → engine (`pathland-engine`) → ring emission chain now works end-to-end, verified by tests. Here's what actually gets emitted for your example:

```rust
let mut root = vstack![text("a"), text("b")].spacing(4.0).padding(8.0).build();
assign_ids(&mut root, &mut 1);
engine.emit(&root, &mut guest);
```

Trace of the emitted 16-byte opcodes (confirmed by `first_emit_produces_full_structure` and `color_property_emits_color_value_type`):

| # | Opcode | Bytes (category/cmd/flags A B C) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `TREE:CREATE_NODE` | `01 01 … 01 … 02 …` | node 1 = VSTACK |
| 2 | `STYLE:SET_PROPERTY` | `02 01 … 01 … F32<<16\|SPACING … 4.0` | spacing = 4 |
| 3 | `STYLE:SET_PROPERTY` | `02 01 … 01 … F32<<16\|PADDING … 8.0` | padding = 8 |
| 4 | `TREE:CREATE_NODE` | `01 01 … 02 … 03 …` | node 2 = TEXT |
| 5 | `TREE:INSERT_CHILD` | `01 03 … 01 … 02 … 00` | 2 into 1 at index 0 |
| 6 | `STYLE:SET_TEXT` | `02 03 … 02 … arenaRef` | node 2 text = "a" |
| 7-9 | … | same pattern for node 3 | TEXT "b" |

**Verified correct details:**
- **Value types** — colors emit `valueType=COLOR (0x07)` (test `color_property_emits_color_value_type`), spacing/padding/fontSize emit `F32` — via `value_type_for()` in pathland-view.
- **Arena text** — `SET_TEXT` writes the string to the bump arena and references it by offset (`host` test decodes it back to `"ab"`).
- **Structural** — `CREATE_NODE`/`INSERT_CHILD` order is parent-first, matches spec vectors.
- **Diffing** — unchanged tree emits zero; a spacing change emits exactly one `SET_PROPERTY`; adds/removes/reorders emit only `INSERT`/`DELETE`/`MOVE`.

One caveat worth noting: **spacing/padding now flow through the generic property map** (since I moved them out of `Component`), so the emitted bytes are `STYLE:SET_PROPERTY` with `valueType=F32` — same as before, but now driven by modifiers instead of stack fields. The opcode stream is unchanged in meaning.

So yes — the DSL generates correct, spec-conformant opcodes today. Ready to commit whenever you are.

parts.text: Committed as `3de55f5`.

I want to reconsinder the next goals defines as issues in the repo. The typescript demo is not important anymore. And Rust desktop app should come before quarkus app. Also, before all that, we need to introduce a transport layer, which defines how the opcodes are transported. Fx. when it is a server rendered aplication for the browser, we want to batch the opcodes to match either a timed interval (fx. 4ms) or a size matching a network frame. But on desktop we want to use shared memory instead.

The user wants to reconsider the POC goals and issue ordering:

1. TypeScript demo (#14) is not important anymore — drop it.
2. Rust desktop app (#16) should come before Quarkus (#15).
3. Before all that, introduce a **transport layer** that defines how opcodes are transported:
   - Server-rendered app for browser: batch opcodes to match a timed interval (e.g. 4ms) or a size matching a network frame.
   - Desktop: shared memory instead.

Let me investigate the current repo state to ground the plan. I should look at:
- Current issues #12-#16
- Current architecture: ring buffer in linear memory, WASM engine
- The spec's memory layout / transport concepts
- Whether there's anything about transport already

Let me think about the transport layer design:

Currently the protocol is: guest engine writes 16-byte opcodes into a ring buffer in shared linear memory, host reads them. For a desktop app with GTK4, the host is a native process (Rust) sharing linear memory — that's the shared memory transport.

For a server-rendered browser app (Quarkus SSR), the guest engine runs server-side, and opcodes must be shipped over WebSocket/HTTP to the browser. There, you want to batch opcodes:

## Linear Memory Layout

The guest engine and host share a **single linear memory**. Regions are fixed at module start:

```
+───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
| 0x0000  Header block (64 B)  — cursors, frame counter, layout  |
| 0x0040  Ring buffer (16 B × slotCount)                         |
| ...      (slots densely packed, 64-byte aligned base)          |
| 0x10040 Arena (bump region for strings / token paths / lists)  |
| ...                                                            |
+───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
```

### Header block (64 bytes)

| Offset | Size | Field | Producer | Description |
|--------|------|-------|----------|-------------|
| 0x00 | 4 | `magic` | — | `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`) |
| 0x04 | 2 | `version` | — | Wire protocol version (1) |
| 0x06 | 4 | `ringOffset` | — | Byte offset of the ring region |
| 0x0A | 4 | `ringBytes` | — | Byte length of the ring region |
| 0x0E | 4 | `slotCount` | — | Number of ring slots (power of two) |
| 0x12 | 4 | `arenaOffset` | — | Byte offset of the arena region |
| 0x14 | 4 | `arenaBytes` | — | Byte length of the arena region |
| 0x18 | 4 | `arenaCursor` | guest | Next free byte in the arena |
| 0x1C | 4 | `readCursor` | host | Ring slot the host has consumed up to |
| 0x20 | 4 | `writeCursor` | guest | Ring slot the guest has written up to |
| 0x24 | 4 | `frameCount` | guest | Monotonic completed-frame counter |
| 0x28 | 36 | reserved | — | Zero |

### Ring buffer

- Contiguous array of **16-byte slots**; `slotCount` is a **power of two** (wrap via mask, no modulo).
- **Producer** (guest) writes at `writeCursor`, then advances `writeCursor` and increments `frameCount` at frame end.
- **Consumer** (host) reads from `readCursor` up to `writeCursor`; after draining a frame it advances `readCursor`.
- **Backpressure**: the producer must not advance `writeCursor` past `readCursor` (ring full). The producer SHOULD flush a frame before the ring is full.
- **Frame boundary detection**: the host watches `frameCount`. When it advances, exactly one frame (all slots from the previously consumed `readCursor` to the current `writeCursor`) is complete.

### Arena

- A pre-allocated **bump region** for variable-length data (strings, token paths).
- Every arena entry is **self-describing**: `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`.
- Opcodes reference entries by their **byte offset** (`arenaRef`), so an entry's length is read directly from the arena — all opcodes stay 16 bytes.
- The guest advances `arenaCursor` monotonically (no free-list, no fragmentation). The arena MAY be reset via `META::RESET`.

---

## Colors

Literal colors are **sRGB** (IEC 61966-2-1, D65 white point), packed as `0xAARRGGBB`:

- `AA`: alpha (0x00 transparent – 0xFF opaque)
- `RR`: red, `GG`: green, `BB`: blue

Stored little-endian in a `u32` payload. Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation remain **renderer-owned** (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)).

---

## Design Token System

### Core Principle

> **The renderer owns the defaults. The application owns the overrides.**

This ensures a native look-and-feel by default and cross-platform consistency when the application overrides tokens.

### Responsibilities

| Aspect | Owner | Responsibility |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| **Default Token Values** | Renderer | Define platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens |
| **Token Overrides** | Application | Specify overrides for cross-platform consistency |
| **Token Resolution** | Renderer | Resolve final token values (override or default) |
| **Platform Adaptation** | Renderer | Adapt default token values to platform conventions |

### Token Identification

Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`, `font.body`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.

## Frame Lifecycle

A frame is a batch of delta opcodes produced by one `emit` pass:

1. Guest begins a frame.
2. Guest emits the delta opcodes (tree structure and/or property changes) into consecutive ring slots.
3. Guest allocates strings in the arena as needed.
4. Guest `end_frame()`: publishes `writeCursor`, then increments `frameCount`.
5. Host observes `frameCount` change, drains `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances `readCursor`.

2. Current: `Guest` writes to shared memory ring, `Host` reads from shared memory ring. This IS the shared-memory transport.
3. For network: need to serialize frames (opcodes + arena strings) into a byte stream, batch them by time (4ms) or size (MTU/network frame), and send over WebSocket.

Actually, the arena is a bump region. The opcodes reference arena entries by absolute offset. For network transport, we need to send the arena region that those opcodes reference. Since the arena cursor only advances, we could send the arena delta since the last frame, but offsets are absolute so the receiver needs to maintain the full arena state. Or send the full arena each time (could be large). Or reset arena on each network frame and send the full arena.

Let me look at how the current implementation handles arena and think about what a transport layer needs.

4. **Ordering/reliability**: WebSocket is ordered reliable; desktop shared memory is synchronous. Transport abstraction should model "send a frame" as an async operation.

Let me look at what the current host does and whether there's already a "describe" function, etc.

3. **Batching**: time-based flush (4ms) + size-based flush. Where does this live? A `NetworkTransport` with a buffer and flush policy.

4. **Is the transport guest-side or host-side or both?** The engine (guest) produces opcodes. In the desktop case, guest and host share memory directly. In the SSR case, the guest runs server-side (in Quarkus via WASM/WIT), produces frames into a buffer, and the transport batches + sends them over WebSocket. pub trait Transport {

}

- A **frame serializer**: opcodes + arena → bytes (`[version][frameCount][opcodeCount][opcodes...][arenaBytes]`).

But for network, we want to send only the arena bytes referenced by the new frame's opcodes, or the arena delta. Since the arena is a bump region shared across frames, absolute offsets... 

Hmm, let me think about the cleanest design for the network transport:

**Network wire format (a "batch"):**
```
[magic u32 "PLPL"][version u16][batchFrameCount u32][opcodeCount u32][arenaLen u32]
[opcodes: opcodeCount * 16 bytes]
[arena: arenaLen bytes]
```

The arena problem: opcodes reference arena offsets. If we send the full arena each time, the receiver rebuilds its arena state from absolute offsets, and offsets are stable across frames (bump region never moves). So sending the FULL arena each batch works and is simple — but wasteful for large arenas. For a POC with small strings, that's acceptable. Alternatively send a delta but then the receiver must maintain the arena and the first frame must establish baseline. Actually since offsets are absolute and stable, the receiver can just keep the last-seen arena and merge. But simplest correct approach: send the arena delta since the last sent frame's arenaCursor, and have the receiver append to its arena buffer. The receiver's arena starts empty and grows; absolute offsets remain valid because the bump region is append-only and offsets never change.

Wait — is the arena ever reset? Spec says "The arena MAY be reset via META::RESET." On reset, arenaCursor = 0 and offsets restart. So the receiver must also handle RESET by clearing its arena. That's handled by META:RESET opcode which the receiver already processes.

So network transport design:
- Sender tracks `last_arena_cursor`. Each batch includes `[arenaDeltaLen][arena bytes from last_arena_cursor..current]`. Receiver appends to its arena buffer.
- Actually even simpler: include the arena delta bytes and the receiver appends. First send: delta from 0 = full arena.

For the POC, maybe simpler to just send opcodes + full-arena-delta. Good.

**Batching:**
- Accumulate opcodes+arena deltas across multiple frames.
- Flush when: (a) time interval elapsed (e.g. 4ms), OR (b) buffered size >= max frame size (e.g. ~1400 bytes TCP/WebSocket frame, or 16KB).
- Provide `flush()` for explicit flush (e.g. after initial render).

This is a solid design. Let me also consider: should the transport be direction-agnostic (also carry EVENT host→guest)? The user's framing: "how the opcodes are transported". I think the plan: extract a `Transport` trait, keep the ring as the shared-memory impl, add the network batch impl + serialization.

The current architecture: guest engine writes 16-byte opcodes into a ring buffer in shared linear memory. Host reads them. This is the "shared memory" transport already — it's the in-process / WASM-shared-memory case.

For a network transport (SSR browser app), we need to:

The whole architecture is WASM-based: the guest engine compiles to wasm32 and runs inside the host process (whether that's a browser, a native Rust process via wasmtime, or a Java/Quarkus process via wasmtime). The ring buffer lives in shared linear memory between the WASM guest and the host.

So the "transport layer" is the abstraction over HOW frames move from producer (guest engine) to consumer (host renderer):
- **Same-process/shared-memory transport**: guest and host share linear memory; ring buffer + arena is the transport. This is what exists today in pathland-opcode (Guest/Host).

So the transport layer would read the frames from shared memory, serialize them (opcodes + arena strings), batch them per timing/size policy, and ship over the socket. So the transport layer has two parts:
1. **Serialization/deserialization**: encode a frame (opcodes + arena delta) into a byte blob, and decode it back. This is important: currently the arena lives in shared memory. For network transport, the strings (text content) must travel with the opcodes. So a transport frame = header + opcodes + arena bytes.

2. **The ring is not a byte transport** — it's a *zero-copy SPSC ring in shared linear memory with cursors and framing in a header block*. Its API is `Host::frames()` → `Vec<Frame>`. Forcing it into a `Transport` trait with a `next_frame()` signature either loses the "batch of frames" semantics or contorts the API.
3. **`std` vs `no_std`**: the ring/host is `no_std`; network transport needs `std` (timers, sockets). A shared `Transport` trait would need to live somewhere both can reach. That's fine (the trait can be in opcode, impls elsewhere), but it forces the trait to be defined at the lowest level.
4. **Lifetimes**: `Frame<'a>` borrows linear memory. A trait method `fn next_frame(&mut self) -> Option<Frame<'_>>` requires GATs — doable but adds complexity for little benefit.
5. **The distinction is architectural, not incidental**: shared memory is synchronous, zero-copy, same-process. Network is asynchronous, serialized, cross-process. They differ in *framing policy* (flush timing, batching) which lives on the network producer side, not in the frame representation.

**My recommendation:**

The ring buffer is *a* transport — the shared-memory transport — but it should stay as-is, embedded in `pathland-opcode`'s linear memory protocol, **because the transport seam is the `Frame` type, not a `Transport` trait.**

- The **unit of transport** is a `Frame` (opcodes + arena delta). This is already transport-neutral and is the right abstraction.
- The **consumer** (`RenderTree::apply_frame`) is already transport-agnostic.
- The ring's `Host`/`Guest` remain the shared-memory framing implementation; the network `BatchEncoder`/`BatchDecoder` become the second framing implementation.
- No `Transport` trait is forced; instead, both backends materialize `Frame`s, and a thin `BatchDecoder` produces `Frame`-compatible views so `apply_frame` works identically.

BUT — I should note there IS one genuinely useful formalization: making `BatchDecoder` output something that `apply_frame` can consume. The cleanest way is to have `BatchDecoder` reconstruct a `Frame`-like view. Since `Frame<'a>` borrows slices, a decoded batch can live in a `Vec<u8>` owned by the decoder, and the decoder hands out `Frame` views borrowing that buffer. That requires `Frame` to be constructible from raw slices — or a small trait/struct that both the ring host and the decoder produce.

So the real design question isn't "should the ring be a transport" — it's "**what is the common denominator that both the ring and the network produce?**" Answer: a `Frame`-shaped view. That's the thing to extract, if anything.

Let me present this analysis and ask the user's preference. Actually the user asked "Do you think it makes best sense to keep the ring buffer as is or to extract it as a transport?"

I should give a clear recommendation. My recommendation: keep the ring as-is, but formalize the frame-view seam. Don't force a `Transport` trait over the ring.

Let me think about whether a `Transport` trait has real value for the future. "potentially more in the future" — what transports could come? 
- In-process shared memory (current ring)
- Network (WebSocket/TCP) — SSR
- Possibly: node.js worker threads (shared ArrayBuffer — still shared memory), WebRTC data channels, pipes to subprocesses, GTK's IPC.

For most of these, the frame-view seam holds: each produces `Frame`-ish data. A trait could be useful for e.g. the desktop app that might want to switch between embedded (same process) and WIT-component (separate module) transports. But that's speculative.

There's a real argument for a minimal trait when the app wants to be transport-agnostic at the API level (e.g., the desktop app code shouldn't care whether the renderer is in-process or via a WIT host). But the POC doesn't need that yet.

I'll present both, recommend keeping ring as-is + formalizing the frame-view seam, and ask.

Let me also consider: the user's instinct "is the ring buffer a transport" is really good — it forces clarity on what "transport" means. I should validate the instinct: yes, conceptually the ring IS the shared-memory transport; but the clean extraction point is the `Frame` unit, and the ring stays as the zero-copy implementation of producing frames from linear memory.

One more consideration: conformance/spec. The spec currently frames the ring as THE transport. If we keep the ring as-is but add network batching, we should document both as transport mechanisms with the shared batch/frame format.

Let me write this up concisely with a recommendation and a question.

Actually, I realize I should think harder about what "extract the ring as a transport" would concretely mean, because there are two levels:

Level 1: **Extract `Frame`/frame-view as the shared seam** (what I recommend). Ring Host produces Frames; BatchDecoder produces Frames; consumer only knows Frame.

Level 2: **Extract a `Transport` trait** that both implement: e.g.
```rust
pub trait Transport {
    fn read_frames(&mut self) -> Vec<Frame>;  // hmm, lifetimes...
}
```
This forces a common interface. Problems: the ring host is no_std, zero-copy, same-process, synchronous; network is owned, batched, async. The interfaces genuinely differ enough that the trait would be thin or leaky.

I think the honest answer: **the ring buffer should NOT be extracted into a Transport trait. It should remain the shared-memory framing implementation. The extraction that makes sense is the `Frame` view — the unit both transports deliver.**

Let me also address: "potentially more in the future" — if we later need transport-agnostic app code, we add a trait at the *consumer boundary* (over `apply_frame`-style functions), not at the ring. 

I'll present this. And ask whether they want me to plan with this framing (keep ring, formalize frame-view seam + BatchDecoder producing frames) or whether they specifically want a Transport trait.

I should be concise but this is an architecture discussion so some depth is warranted.

Excellent question to resolve now — it defines the crate boundaries. Here's my analysis, grounded in the actual code.

## The key insight: the transport seam already exists at `Frame`, not at the ring

Look at the consumer boundary (`pathland-host`):

```rust
pub fn apply_frame(&mut self, frame: &Frame<'_>) { ... }   // line 56
```

`apply_frame` is **already transport-agnostic**. It doesn't know — or care — whether the `Frame` came from the ring, a socket, or anything else. A `Frame` (opcodes iterator + arena access, `pathland-opcode` lib.rs:226-261) is the **unit of transport**.

So the ring buffer is *functionally* the shared-memory transport today, but the correct abstraction point is the **frame**, not a `Transport` trait.

## The two candidate designs

**A. Keep the ring as-is + make the network side speak `Frame` too (my recommendation)**

- Ring's `Host::frames()` materializes `Frame` views from linear memory (zero-copy).
- New `BatchDecoder` materializes `Frame` views from decoded batch bytes (owns its buffer, hands out borrowing `Frame` views).
- Both produce the same `Frame`; `apply_frame` consumes both unchanged.
- No `Transport` trait needed — the `Frame` type *is* the seam.

**B. Extract a `Transport` trait; ring implements it**

```rust
pub trait Transport {
    fn next_frame(&mut self) -> Option<Frame<'_>>;   // needs GATs for the lifetime
}
```

## Why I'd keep the ring as-is (not extract a trait)

1. **The ring isn't a byte transport — it's a zero-copy SPSC ring coupled to the linear-memory protocol** (header block + cursors + arena region, `spec/OPCODE.md:214-244`). Its `Host` returns *batches* of frames (`Vec<Frame>`) with frameCount coalescing semantics. Forcing it into `next_frame()` either loses those semantics or contorts the API.
2. **`no_std` vs `std`**: ring/host is `no_std`; network needs `std` (timers, sockets). A shared trait must live at the lowest level and be reachable by both — doable, but the trait ends up thin because the two really are different animals (synchronous + zero-copy vs asynchronous + serialized).
3. **Lifetimes**: `Frame<'a>` borrows linear memory; `next_frame(&mut self) -> Option<Frame<'_>>` needs GATs. Complexity for a seam that already exists at `Frame`.
4. **The architectural difference is real**: shared memory has no framing policy (flush when written); network has batching policy (time/size). That policy belongs on the *producer* side, not in a shared frame interface.

## The one thing worth formalizing

The genuinely useful extraction is making `BatchDecoder` output **`Frame`-compatible views** so `apply_frame` runs identically. Concretely: `Frame` is constructed from slices (`slots`, `arena`, `start`, `end`) — give the decoder a way to produce `Frame` views over its decoded buffer (or a tiny common trait over `opcodes()` + `arena_get()`). That's the real seam.

## Future transports

If you later want transport-agnostic app code (e.g. the GTK app not caring whether the renderer is in-process or a WIT host), add a trait at the **consumer boundary** (over `apply_frame`-style consumption), not over the ring. The ring stays the shared-memory framing implementation.

**Recommendation:** keep the ring buffer exactly as it is; formalize the `Frame`-view seam and build `BatchEncoder`/`BatchDecoder` to speak that same `Frame` language. This gives you network + shared-memory as peer transports through a common consumer, without contorting the proven zero-copy path.

Confirmed. Here's the finalized plan with the "keep ring; share Frame seam" architecture.

## Plan: Opcode transport layer + goal reordering

### Phase 1 — Issue & doc reorder
1. Close issue **#14** (TS demo) via `gh issue close 14 --reason "not planned"`.
2. Create new issue **"POC Goal: Opcode transport layer"** with scope below, slotted after #13.
3. **`AGENTS.md`** — reorder POC Goals table: #12 Complete, #13 In progress, **NEW transport (next)**, #16 GTK desktop, #15 Quarkus, drop #14. Update deferred list (remove "TS browser demo").
4. **`README.md`** — reorder roadmap list to match (opcode engine, components, transport, GTK desktop, Quarkus SSR).

### Phase 2 — `pathland-transport` crate (new workspace member, depends on `pathland-opcode`)

**Core principle:** the `Frame` type is the transport seam. The ring (`Host::frames()`) stays untouched; the network side produces `Frame`-compatible views so `apply_frame` works identically.

**Batch wire format** (documented in new `spec/OPCODE.md` "Transport" section + `CONFORMANCE.md` vectors):

```
magic "PLPL" (u16) | version (u16) | frameCount (u32) | opcodeCount (u32)
| opcodes (16 B × opcodeCount) | arenaDeltaLen (u32) | arena delta bytes
```

**Components:**
- `BatchEncoder` — serializes opcodes + arena **delta** (since last batch, tracked via cursor) into `Vec<u8>`; successive batches carry only appended arena bytes.
- `BatchDecoder` — parses a batch into opcodes + arena delta, appends to a mirrored arena, and produces a `Frame`-compatible view over its buffer so `RenderTree::apply_frame` consumes it unchanged. *(Requires a small `Frame` constructor or a shared view trait — `Frame` fields are currently private.)*
- `BatchPolicy { max_interval: Duration, max_batch_bytes: usize }` — defaults **4ms / 1400B**; time-based (since first buffered opcode) and size-based flush, first trigger wins.
- `Batcher` — buffers encoded frames against the policy; `push_frame()` + `flush()`.

**`std` boundary:** `BatchPolicy`/`Batcher` use `std::time` (timers); `BatchEncoder`/`BatchDecoder` core stays `no_std` + `alloc`. So `pathland-transport` is `std` overall — matching the network/host side. Shared-memory remains `no_std` in `pathland-opcode`.

### Phase 3 — Tests & conformance
- Golden batch vectors in `CONFORMANCE.md` + mirror test (round-trip: encode → decode → same opcodes + arena strings).
- Batcher tests: time-trigger (tiny interval), size-trigger (tiny `max_batch_bytes`), first-wins.
- Decoder → `apply_frame` integration test (decode a batch, feed `RenderTree`).
- Full `cargo test` + wasm32 build; update AGENTS test count.

### Phase 4 — Verify
`cargo test`, `cargo clippy`, wasm32 build per AGENTS.md.

**Scope guardrail:** events over the wire are left as a documented hook (reverse channel in the batch format), not implemented — events remain deferred. `BatchDecoder` stays ring-free; no changes to `pathland-opcode` beyond the `Frame` constructor/view trait needed for the seam.
